7.text: The inhabitants of Luˊᵋren, Yaˊnřa-ñai, and other villages and camps around

8.text: St. Lawrence Bay, are famed for their roughness. Some of them buy from

9.text: American whalers revolvers, which they carry in a special pocket up the sleeve,

10.text: ready to handle. Mr. J. Kelly, the American agent for buying reindeer, who spent

11.text: the winter of 1897-98 on the shores of St. Lawrence Bay, in a block-house built

12.text: for the purpose near the village Yaˊnřa-ñai, had considerable trouble with the

13.text: natives; and I heard that an attempt was made to attack his house and to rob it.

14.text: The Chukchee cannot be called quick-witted, especially in trading-transactions,

15.text: in which they are easily imposed upon by their neighbors. Their system of

16.text: calculation is quinary-vigesimal, but very imperfect, and all numerical operations

17.text: are performed with the help of the fingers of both hands. The word for

18.text: counting means literally “I finger” (t-rɪˊlhɪrkɪn). The question “How many?”

19.text: runs “How many fingers?” (Ter rɪˊlhɪt?) The numbers proceed in the way

20.text: usual to many primitive languages, so that mɪˊʟɪñên (“five”) is shortened from

21.text: mɪng̣ɪˊʟɪñɪn (“hand”); mɪng̣ɪˊtkên (“ten”) signifies “belonging to two hands;”

22.text: kɪlhɪˊnkɪn (“fifteen”) is probably contracted from g̣ɪtkaˊlhɪkên (“belonging to

23.text: the foot”); qliˊkkin (“twenty”) signifies “belonging to a man.” The word qlaˊul

24.text: (“man”) is also used frequently for “twenty.” The fingers and toes play such

25.text: a prominent part in counting, that I doubt whether a Chukchee would be able

26.text: to make a calculation without them. The larger numbers are composed of

27.text: groups of “twenty” (“man”). They are also counted on the fingers, so that

28.text: the limit of enumeration is “twenty scores” (qlik-qliˊkkin). All numbers above

30.text: This term is also applied by a few rich traders to express the idea of

31.text: “one thousand.” Many of the people, especially the Reindeer men, are unable

32.text: to deal with as high a number as a couple of scores. Therefore when dealing

33.text: in small skins, like those of fawns, squirrels, etc., which are traded in large

34.text: numbers, they tie them in bunches and trade off each bunch or small group

35.text: of bunches by itself. Squirrel-skins are tied in tens after the manner of the

36.text: Lamut; the fawn-skins are done up in threes (the usual barter price of a piece

37.text: of compressed tea, called a “brick”) or in fives; then four bunches are fastened

39.text: In recent years the Chukchee traders, and especially the collectors of

40.text: tribute, in imitation of the Russians, have begun to use small notched sticks

41.text: as tallies, every notch representing one five, and the fourth notch being marked

42.text: out by a deeper cut to indicate a score.
